Actual Article Body:
We’ve learned that ignoring the hip pocket is a big mistake. Australia would benefit from a courageous reset of economic and social policy

Wouldn’t it be nice, as the Beach Boys sang, if the US midterm election results represented a return to kindness?

It would be a fitting closing of the circle, given that Hillary Clinton campaigned on a “love Trumps hate” platform in 2016. It certainly didn’t back then, and I doubt it did two weeks ago despite the Democrats being quick to claim the results as a return to civility and care.

The brutal reality is that Donald Trump and his Republican backers were slapped with a hard backhander from Americans, resentful that his self-indulgent economic and foreign policies have hit them in the back pocket and at the gas pump.

Australians are not immune to the consequences of his reckless adventures but our predicament is also of our own making, not totally the result of Trump’s ill-thought-out war in Iran.

Forthcoming Australian elections will test the theory of niceness over hip pocket.

But the dynamics are somewhat different.

In the US, voters have a simple choice between red and blue. We now live in a multipartisan environment, whether Anthony Albanese and Angus Taylor like it or not.

Casting around for an alternative to Trumpism, be it due to his mean politics or economic mistakes, the only alternative for voters in the US was to vote Democrat or not vote at all. The choice was clearcut.

Not so here, or across the ditch as the New Zealand election results foreshadowed last weekend. Australians have more options and the political environment is fluid.

In New Zealand, the incumbent, centre-right Luxon government is clinging on at best, blaming the global impact of the war in Iran on cost of living. As in Australia this has fed voter rancour and for the first time neither of New Zealand’s major parties won more than 30% of the vote.

The new centrist Opportunity party, explicitly inspired by the success of community independents in Australia, won an extraordinary seven seats from a standing start, while the libertarian ACT won 13 and the populist, anti-immigration New Zealand First won 12.

There is no simple path to power for either major party and neither coalition bloc has a majority. Those in the centrist Opportunity party may be the kingmakers.
